--- title: "Tables" guide-section: "Using tinytab" bread-crumbs: false --- A [`Table`](../reference/Table.qmd) holds data in columns, and renders it as text or HTML. ## Creating a table Pass a dictionary that maps each column name to a list of values. All the columns must have the same length: ::: {#583e0605 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from tinytab import Table menu = Table( { "item": ["coffee", "bagel", "croissant"], "price": [3.5, 2.25, 4.0], "sold": [120, 45, None], } ) menu.columns, menu.n_rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (['item', 'price', 'sold'], 3) ``` ::: ::: In a notebook, or on a page like this one, a table displays as HTML. Missing values (`None`) show as empty cells: ::: {#5003f6e2 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} menu ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
itempricesold
coffee3.5120
bagel2.2545
croissant4.0
``` ::: ::: ## Formatting columns [`Table.fmt()`](../reference/Table.fmt.qmd) attaches a formatting function to a column. Any function that takes a value and returns a string works, including tinytab's own formatters: ::: {#2c849664 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from tinytab import fmt_currency menu.fmt("price", fmt_currency) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
itempricesold
coffee$3.50120
bagel$2.2545
croissant$4.00
``` ::: ::: `fmt()` returns a *new* table and leaves the original unchanged, so calls can be chained, one per column: ::: {#e340f30f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from tinytab import fmt_number menu.fmt("price", fmt_currency).fmt("sold", lambda x: fmt_number(x, decimals=0)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
itempricesold
coffee$3.50120
bagel$2.2545
croissant$4.00
``` ::: ::: Formatters are never given missing values, so a formatter doesn't need to handle `None`. ## Rendering as text [`Table.as_text()`](../reference/Table.as_text.qmd) renders a Markdown-style text table, ready to print or paste into a Markdown document: ::: {#9a071952 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(menu.fmt("price", fmt_currency).as_text()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` | item | price | sold | |-----------|-------|------| | coffee | $3.50 | 120 | | bagel | $2.25 | 45 | | croissant | $4.00 | | ``` ::: ::: ## Rendering as HTML [`Table.as_html()`](../reference/Table.as_html.qmd) returns the HTML as a string, for use in a web page or report: ::: {#2446ce62 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(menu.fmt("price", fmt_currency).as_html()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```
itempricesold
coffee$3.50120
bagel$2.2545
croissant$4.00
``` ::: ::: Every value is HTML-escaped, so text in the data can never be mistaken for markup: ::: {#611d8637 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} Table({"name": ["bold", "Tom & Jerry"]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
name
<b>bold</b>
Tom & Jerry
``` ::: ::: ## Saving and loading [`Table.to_csv()`](../reference/Table.to_csv.qmd) writes the table's values to a CSV file, and [`Table.from_csv()`](../reference/Table.from_csv.qmd) reads one back: ::: {#92693059 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import tempfile from pathlib import Path path = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "menu.csv" menu.to_csv(path) Table.from_csv(path) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
itempricesold
coffee3.5120
bagel2.2545
croissant4.0
``` ::: ::: Two things to know about CSV files: - Formatting isn't saved. `to_csv()` writes the original values, not the formatted ones. - CSV files don't record types, so `from_csv()` reads every value as a string.
